title: My first property lost value and I hate living there. Should I buy another?
excerpt: A buyer whose Setapak condo fell in value, with a short-stay unit also bought, is shortlisting a third project. Sean says stop buying, rent out the condo and fix how you choose properties first.

question.asker: From KF, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: KF bought a subsale condo in Setapak for RM510,000, using most of his savings, and it is now worth about RM400,000 to RM450,000; the rent wouldn't cover the loan without partitions. Last year he also bought into a project near KLCC meant for short-stay rentals. Construction noise from a new development opposite drove him out of the Setapak condo to a family member's home, and he is now choosing between three new projects near train lines.
question.text: Which new project should he buy, should he stay with family or move out, and should he rent out or sell the Setapak unit?

answer.quote: Buying the property is not the solution.
answer.summary: Stop buying for now. Rent out the Setapak unit so the tenant pays much of the instalment, stay with family or rent elsewhere, and decide whether to sell once the project opposite is finished and priced. Before any third purchase, fix the way he picks properties: check median prices and real rents first, and settle on one clear intent.

reasons.title: Property doesn't always make money
reasons.body: Even a subsale bought at the wrong price can lose value. Not buying only means missing a chance to make money, while buying wrongly can wipe out years of savings.

reasons.title: Check the numbers before, not after
reasons.body: Compare the price with the area's median price per square foot, and look up what tenants actually pay nearby before buying, not after. Sean is happy if rent covers about 90% of an investment's instalment, or 85% for a home you may later rent out.

reasons.title: Wanting everything means no clear intent
reasons.body: Near a train line, easy to rent, good for short stays and good to live in: that list is every goal at once. A third residential loan is also capped at 70%, so the next purchase needs a much larger down payment.

reasons.title: Short-stay buildings need an exit plan
reasons.body: Sean prefers units that can be let several ways. Short-stay rules can change, as in Penang, hotel-style buildings have lost money before, and the only buyer later is another investor.

actions: Rent out the Setapak unit rather than leaving it empty, and furnish it well enough to attract tenants.
If you stay with family, pay them a fair rent or share the bills, or rent a place of your own.
Wait until the project opposite is finished, compare its prices with yours, then decide whether to sell.
Before buying again, check each project's median price per square foot and real rents nearby.
Decide whether your next home is to live in or to invest, and judge projects against that one intent.
caveat: Construction noise is part of development and is usually limited to permitted hours, so Sean doesn't blame the developer. If the project opposite sells for more than his unit, holding on may be the better choice.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #253. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in June 2024. The episode was sponsored by PropertyGuru's Brickz home report, a paid transaction report Sean says he uses; median prices can also be checked free on its website.
